Every system in the corpus follows this approach, even though repository-level retrieval over code is a well-studied area: RepoCoder [60], RepoBench [61], and CrossCodeEval [62] all build retrieval pipelines for code, and Long Code Arena [64] provides matching long-context evaluation. Wang et al.’s CodeRAG-Bench [63] asks the very question this section raises, “can retrieval augment code generation?”, and finds gains that are highly variable across tasks: substantial for documentation-lookup and library-use scenarios but marginal or absent for tasks where the model already has sufficient parametric knowledge. The inconsistency of these gains may help explain why production SWE agents skip the RAG layer entirely rather than investing in task-dependent retrieval routing. The reasons are domain-specific. Code carries dense deterministic structural metadata—file paths, language servers, tree-sitter parses, type information—that semantic-similarity retrieval cannot replicate (and that structure-aware tools such as RepoAgent [65] and Aider’s RepoMap exploit directly). Code changes minute to minute, so pre-indexed embeddings are stale almost by construction. Every coding environment already ships a near-optimal retrieval system in the form of ripgrep, find, and glob. On the typical SWE-agent task, RAG adds operational cost (embedding compute, vector-store maintenance, drift management) without offering marginal value.

Observation 9. Two technologies that the broader LLM-application literature treats as central are missing from all eleven systems—a finding that survived a threefold corpus expansion and a three-month re-audit. No system uses a general-purpose agentic framework in its agent runtime (LangChain, LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI, or any of a dozen others checked; Gemini CLI uses neither of Google’s own); every loop is hand-rolled in the host language’s async primitives, with OpenCode’s use of a provider-abstraction SDK for inner plumbing as the closest boundary case. No system uses vector-embedding RAG for code retrieval; all rely on ripgrep, tree-sitter, glob, and auto-discovered Markdown context files, and where conversation-scale recall is needed, the production answer is lexical search (Hermes’s SQLite FTS5) or, in exactly one default configuration (OpenClaw), hybrid embeddings over chat history—never over the source tree. Production harnesses operate on a different complexity budget from generic LLM applications: debuggability and prompt transparency outweigh framework reuse when the failure mode is mutating real code. Section 14.2 gives the absence its historical resolution.

Observation 10. The architectural patterns described in Anthropic’s Effective Agents engineering series (December 2024 through September 2025) line up closely with the architectures observed across the four provider-native systems, which were built independently. Whether this reflects shared empirical reality, public-guidance influence, or both is an open question.

13.3 Inter-Agent Protocols: Outward Adoption, Inward In-Process

The twin absences are about two technologies that simply do not appear in the corpus. Inter-agent protocols (ACP, A2A) follow a different pattern again—and this is the dimension that moved most between our snapshots. ACP now ships as a first-class production dependency or implementation in six of the eleven systems: Mistral Vibe (agent-client-protocol==0.10.1, with session fork, workspace trust, and rewind exposed over the protocol), OpenClaw (gateway translator), OpenCode (opencode acp serves the agent side over stdio), Hermes (ACP adapter and registry modules), OpenHands (an ACPAgent class, discussed below), and Gemini CLI (whose A2A module is a separate protocol for the mesh role). Outside the corpus, xAI’s Grok Build launched with a documented ACP server mode on day one (Section 3.7; vendor-documented, not source-verified). None of the corpus adoptions is experimental.

What is interesting is the placement—and ACP now occupies three distinct architectural roles:

  1. 1.

    Editor ↔\leftrightarrow agent (outward server). The LSP role for ACP [41]: Zed, JetBrains, and other IDEs drive a local agent as they would a language server. Mistral Vibe, OpenCode, Hermes, OpenClaw, and Grok Build all serve this boundary.

  2. 2.

    Agent-as-backend (inward host). The role nobody held in April: OpenHands’s ACPAgent delegates its step() to an external ACP server, with provider metadata for pinned claude-agent-acp, codex-acp, and gemini --acp binaries—rival harnesses become interchangeable brains inside an OpenHands conversation. The meta-harness of Section 14.4 drives its Goose and Qwen adapters the same way (and taps Kiro’s ACP permission stream while driving its TUI), and Hermes consumes an ACP agent as a model transport (GitHub Copilot’s CLI as a chat backend). The protocol built for editors turned out to be the interface for hosting.

  3. 3.

    Cross-vendor mesh (A2A [42]). Still Gemini CLI’s alone in the corpus: a remote orchestrator drives a local Gemini CLI as one node in a multi-vendor topology, now with usage metadata over the wire.

Table 14 lists the communication mechanism each multi-agent system uses between a main agent and its own sub-agents, alongside its protocol roles.

The inward/outward split of the April edition survives in refined form. For coordinating their own sub-agents, eight of the nine multi-agent systems still use in-process primitives or, where they cross processes, something other than the standard protocols: Pi’s extension spawns OS processes speaking plain JSONL, and Hermes’s swarm coordinates through a SQLite blackboard. What changed is the inward consumption of whole harnesses: hosting a rival agent as a swappable backend—OpenHands’s ACP hosting, Hermes’s ACP-as-model-transport, the meta-harness’s adapter fleet—is a production pattern that did not exist in April, and ACP is its lingua franca. Pi adds a final nuance: it rejects the standard protocols yet invents a proprietary outward RPC for the same embedding role—evidence that the outward-facing protocol pressure is real even where the standards are declined.

Observation 11. Inter-agent protocol placement has evolved from a two-role story (outward: editor integration and mesh; inward: nothing) to a three-role story. ACP ships in six of eleven systems and now serves (1) its designed editor↔\leftrightarrowagent boundary, (2) a role outside the protocol’s design brief—harness hosting, where OpenHands runs Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini CLI as interchangeable step-backends and Hermes consumes an ACP agent as a model transport—and (3) via A2A, still only in Gemini CLI, the cross-vendor mesh. For a harness’s own sub-agents, eight of nine multi-agent systems still use in-process primitives or, where they cross processes, something other than the standard protocols (Pi’s JSONL extension, Hermes’s SQLite-blackboard swarm); OpenClaw’s ACP spawn is the lone case that routes sub-agent coordination over a standard protocol. The practitioner guidance sharpens accordingly: build an ACP server (it now buys you editors, hosts, and meta-orchestrators at once); keep your sub-agents in-process; and treat A2A as a bet on a cross-vendor mesh whose at-scale demand remains unproven.

13.4 Trade-off Framework

We formalize five fundamental trade-off axes:

Axis 1: Simplicity vs. Capability.

Mini-SWE-Agent’s minimal scaffold reportedly achieves 74%+ on SWE-Bench Verified, while Codex’s far larger codebase reports 69.1%. These figures are not directly comparable (different underlying models, different evaluation runs, different deployment configurations: Mini-SWE-Agent is unsandboxed and Codex is sandboxed) and we do not draw a head-to-head conclusion from them. What the gap does illustrate, qualitatively, is that the additional code in Codex is not invested in raw task-completion logic: a substantial share goes into safety (cross-platform sandboxing), user experience (TUI, streaming), extensibility (MCP, plugins), and robustness. Whether the production scaffolding produces measurable improvements on the same benchmark under matched conditions is an open question that this study does not answer (see Section 15 on threats to validity).

Axis 2: Safety vs. Autonomy.

Systems with more safety infrastructure (Codex, Claude Code) impose more friction on agent actions. Systems with less safety (Mini-SWE-Agent, Aider) enable faster execution but are unsuitable for enterprise deployment without additional safeguards.

Axis 3: Provider Coupling vs. Agnosticism.

Claude Code and Codex exploit provider-specific features (prompt caching, extended thinking, model-specific prompts) at the cost of vendor lock-in. LiteLLM-based systems sacrifice these optimizations for provider flexibility.

Axis 4: Monolithic vs. Modular.

Codex’s 126-crate, million-line Rust workspace optimizes for type safety and performance. Mini-SWE-Agent’s single-file agent maximizes comprehensibility. Pi relocates the entire axis into runtime composition: a minimal core plus an extension event bus. OpenClaw’s plugin SDK and OpenCode’s client/server split enable extensibility and embeddability respectively. Each point on this spectrum serves different user populations.

Axis 5: Scaffold Complexity vs. Model Capability.

This is the most philosophically interesting axis. Mini-SWE-Agent’s competitive benchmark performance demonstrates that current models are capable enough to succeed with minimal scaffolding. Production systems invest in scaffolding not because models need it for task completion, but because users need it for safety, reliability, and workflow integration.

14 The Platform Turn

The preceding sections dissected the harness as an artifact. This section argues that the artifact has changed category: between 2025 and mid-2026, the coding-agent harness completed a turn from tool to platform—a runtime with its own extension ecosystem, package economics, governance layers, switching costs, and, since June 2026, its own meta-layer. The April edition of this study advanced a cautious version of this claim as the “CLI-as-framework hypothesis.” The evidence accumulated since—in the corpus’s own source trees, in the vendor SDKs, and in the market—lets us state it as a thesis.

14.1 From Hypothesis to Thesis: The CLI as Framework

The standard reading of the absence of LangChain, AutoGen, and the rest (Observation 13.2) is that production harnesses do not need frameworks. But there is a second reading: they do not need frameworks because the harness is itself the framework—the default orchestration layer through which developers ship software, not merely a tool they query.

Consider what a framework traditionally provides: a loop, a tool registry, a memory layer, a configuration surface, an extension mechanism. Every one of these is present in every production system studied here. Claude Code ships a streaming ReAct loop, 43 registered tools, a compaction-based memory manager, CLAUDE.md-driven configuration, MCP for integrations and Skills for capability bundles—and Codex, Gemini CLI, Mistral Vibe, Hermes, and OpenCode do the same, each in its own idiom (Pi matches every element but MCP, which it pointedly rejects in favor of CLI tools plus its extension bus). The difference is that the “framework” is not a library the developer imports into their code; it is a runtime the developer works inside of. The developer’s “program” is a natural-language task plus a tree of Markdown files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md, SKILL.md) that configure the agent’s behavior, tool access, and domain knowledge. The “API” is the filesystem, the terminal, and git.

Four convergent signals from the corpus support this reading.

Signal 1: Skills as declarative programs.

Nine of the eleven systems implement Skills (Observation 12.5): directories containing a SKILL.md with instructions, optional scripts, and metadata. A skill is, functionally, a program written for an LLM runtime rather than for a CPU runtime. It declares what the agent should do (SKILL.md body), when it should activate (paths frontmatter in Claude Code, PathTrigger rules in OpenHands, requires in OpenClaw), and what tools it may use. This is the structural analogue of a plugin in a traditional framework, except the programming language is English plus YAML frontmatter—and the layer now has registries, supply-chain security, and agent authors (Section 12.5).

Signal 2: Hooks and event buses as the extension substrate.

In April, user-facing lifecycle hooks were a Claude Code distinctive. By July they are the dominant extension substrate—nine of the eleven systems, with only Aider and Mini-SWE-Agent abstaining: Codex ships hooks whose event names are verbatim Claude Code’s; OpenHands wires pre_tool_use/post_tool_use/stop hooks into Agent.step(), with an agent allowed as a hook handler; Mistral Vibe added hooks.toml shell hooks (deny, rewrite inputs, append context) alongside its internal middleware pipeline; Gemini CLI exposes eleven loop-lifecycle events to extensions; Pi is an event bus, with ∼\sim33 typed events spanning tool interception to raw provider I/O; OpenCode’s plugins are functions returning twenty typed hooks. This is the same extension model that web frameworks and build systems have used for decades, applied to an LLM execution loop. The developer is not writing for the agent; they are writing inside it.

Signal 3: The disappearing boundary between tool and workflow.

In a traditional development workflow, the developer writes code, runs tests, reads logs, commits, and opens PRs as discrete steps. In a harness workflow, these steps are delegated to the agent via natural-language instructions and executed through the agent’s tool system. The agent loop is the workflow engine: Claude Code’s coordinator phases, Codex’s update_plan tool and /goal workflows, OpenHands’s judge-audited goal loop. When the developer types a task and the agent spawns sub-agents, dispatches tools, manages context, and produces the result, the CLI has subsumed the role of the build system, the task runner, and the IDE.

Signal 4: The harness as a service surface.

The clearest post-April signal: harnesses now ship the interfaces of platforms. OpenCode embeds an HTTP server publishing an OpenAPI spec and a generated SDK, with every UI—TUI, desktop, web, IDE plugin, CI action—as a client. OpenHands exposes conversations through an OpenAI-compatible gateway, so any tooling that can call a chat-completions endpoint can drive an agent: the agent as a model. Mistral Vibe teleports local sessions to a hosted runtime; Claude Code pairs its SDK with a hosted Managed Agents API. A runtime with clients, SDKs, and hosted tiers is not a tool with an ecosystem; it is a platform with distribution.

14.2 The Harness–Framework Merger

If the harness is the framework, the two artifact categories should merge—and in 2026 they are merging, visibly, from both directions (Table 15).

Both directions converge on the same artifact shape—loop + tools + skills + sub-agents + hooks + MCP + sessions—whether one starts from a terminal product or from an orchestration library. The convergence is itself validation: when LangChain, the framework whose absence from every harness runtime Observation 13.2 documents, finally built a harness, it independently adopted the corpus’s conventions (SKILL.md progressive disclosure, AGENTS.md memory, sub-agent spawning, todo planning). And the meta-harness of the next subsection completes the picture from above: its baseline installation imports claude-agent-sdk and openai-agents as production dependencies—the “frameworks” a 2026 orchestration layer builds on are the harness SDKs. The twin absence of 2025-era frameworks thus gets its historical resolution: harnesses did not adopt the frameworks; they replaced them, became importable themselves, and turned the question “which agentic framework should I use?” into “which harness do you already run?”

14.3 Platform Economics: Marketplaces, Switching Costs, Governance

Three developments from the ninety-day window are textbook platform economics.

Marketplaces.

Codex grew a plugin marketplace (GitHub/git/URL sources, in-conversation install approval, workspace sharing); skills registries appeared in four systems with trust tiers, provenance verification, and quarantine (Section 12.5); OpenClaw externalized its official plugins to npm. Capability distribution now has app-store mechanics—including the app store’s security pathologies, as SkillProbe’s audit of published skills shows [89].

Switching costs.

Codex ships a first-class importer for Claude Code’s on-disk state: it detects ~/.claude/projects session JSONL files, converts them into Codex rollout items under an import ledger, and offers to translate ~/.claude/settings.json into ~/.codex/config.toml. Vendors writing importers for each other’s session stores is the stage of platform competition where user data becomes the moat—and the countervailing force is equally visible: OpenCode reads Claude Code’s skills directory, OpenHands reads Claude Code’s plugin manifests and hosts rival harnesses outright, and the meta-harness arbitrages every vendor’s lock-in mechanisms into its adapter surface.

Enterprise governance.

Codex’s configuration stack now extends above the user—MDM-managed preferences, host-wide system files, and enterprise cloud-delivered bundles feed both base defaults and a constraint engine that can hard-restrict what user and project scopes may set. Google, meanwhile, announced Gemini CLI’s transition toward an Antigravity-branded CLI—closed-source, where Gemini CLI is Apache-2.0 (Section 3.7)—and withdrew its consumer free tier, and the SpaceX–xAI merger plus the announced $60B Cursor acquisition (pending as of July 2026) priced the harness layer at acquisition scale. Governance layers, gated tiers, and acquisition-scale pricing are the signatures of platforms, not of standalone tools.

14.4 The Meta-Harness Layer

Omnigent [25] is not a twelfth harness; it is a bet that the harness has become a commodity component and that the durable value sits one layer up. Databricks open-sourced it in June 2026 (Apache 2.0, ∼\sim1M lines total, ∼\sim312K of production Python): a four-tier process topology (server ⇄\rightleftarrows host daemon ⇄\rightleftarrows runner ⇄\rightleftarrows per-conversation harness subprocess) whose adapter boundary is, by explicit design, a recursive subset of Omnigent’s own public REST API. Its registry ships 23 canonical harness adapters (plus 16 aliases and a community entry-point group) spanning Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Hermes, Pi, Goose, Qwen, Kimi, Kiro, Copilot, and Antigravity, formalized into five integration modes (sdk-in-process, cli-subprocess, acp-subprocess, native-tui, native-server)—and the declared capabilities are reconciled against a conformance bench (probes for basic turns, tool calling, streaming, interrupts, model override, policy denial), with live verification landed for the four flagship SDK adapters and best-effort declarations for the rest. Harnesses are tested like hardware.

Above that boundary the meta-layer adds four things no single harness provides. Composition: any registry harness is addressable as a sub-agent session of any other, so a Claude-brained orchestrator can dispatch work to Codex and have Cursor review it. Cross-harness policy: one three-level policy plane (session →\to agent →\to admin; six phases; CEL (Common Expression Language), Python, or LLM-classifier evaluators; cross-session per-user budgets) enforced on foreign harnesses through each vendor’s own extension mechanism—Claude Code hooks, Cursor hooks, Hermes hooks, ACP permission requests—with fail-closed semantics. The lock-in mechanisms of Observation 7.1 become, from one layer up, an adapter surface. A uniform sandbox and egress stack: bubblewrap-plus-seccomp on Linux, generated Seatbelt profiles on macOS, Job Objects on Windows—the same architecture the corpus documents inside Codex, re-implemented at the meta-layer, plus an L7 MITM egress proxy (own CA, per-host rules, default-deny) hosting a secretless credential proxy, where real tokens never enter the sandbox and synthetic placeholders are swapped for credentials in flight—a design Codex also ships (its network-proxy crate), here lifted to the meta-layer across all wrapped harnesses. Shareable sessions: server-durable transcripts with multi-device sync, ACL grants, review comments, fork, and mid-session harness switching.

Just as informative is what it does not do: it implements no editing loop, no repository context, no edit-application strategy—the anatomy’s D3/D4 core stays below the line—and it does not pretend the harnesses are equivalent: per-harness capability records, vendor-specific webhook endpoints, a Claude-specific todos field, and a Codex-only goal-mode extension leak through the “common” API by design. Its flagship example, Polly, is a cross-vendor coordinator-worker: a Claude Code-brained orchestrator that writes no code, fans work out to six vendor harnesses in per-task git worktrees, and mandates cross-vendor review in its orchestrator prompt—the reviewer must be a different vendor than the implementer (the mechanism-layer guardrails gate fan-out and blast radius, not vendor identity). Even its restraint is informative: sandboxing is applied inconsistently by design (it exec-wraps the Claude CLI in its own sandbox but delegates to Codex’s native sandbox modes), evidence that OS-level isolation resists being factored out as a shared service. And the twin absences hold at the meta-layer: no agentic framework, no RAG, in a million lines—unless one counts its two baseline dependencies, claude-agent-sdk and openai-agents, which is precisely the point of Section 14.2.

14.5 Ninety Days of Harness Evolution

Because the eight systems of the April edition were re-pinned rather than replaced, the corpus contains a controlled longitudinal sample: the same harnesses, source-diffed across one quarter. Four movements characterize the window.

Convergence became imitation.

April’s convergences were mostly independent rediscovery; July’s are traceable. Codex adopted Claude Code’s hook event vocabulary verbatim and its plan-mode ergonomics; OpenHands adopted Claude Code’s plugin manifest format, its task-tool signature, and its static/dynamic cache boundary; OpenCode reads Claude Code’s skills directory; Hermes’s source comments credit OpenCode (edit matcher), Codex (smart approvals), OpenClaw (orchestrator prompt), and Goose (context hints). Cross-harness lineage is now written in the code itself.

Patterns diffused down the corpus.

Deferred tool loading went from one system to three (plus seven skills variants); read-only plan modes from two to all four provider-native systems; LLM approval classifiers from one (Claude Code) to two (Codex’s Guardian); turn-level checkpointing from one (Mistral Vibe) to three; safety-aware scheduler partitioning from one to two. The half-life of a competitive distinctive in this field is currently measurable in weeks.

Policy migrated out of prose.

The clearest rhetorical trend of the quarter (Observation 7.3): Codex’s newest model prompts dropped the no-commit and anti-gold-plating rules in favor of feature flags; Mistral Vibe deleted its “Never Commit” hard rule and re-founded its prompt on a seven-level precedence contract, A/B-tested server-side; OpenHands teaches commit mechanics. As models internalize norms and harnesses grow governance surfaces, behavioral policy is moving from the prompt (where the model reads it) to configuration (where the platform enforces it).

The trees themselves moved at platform speed.

Codex’s workspace nearly doubled (621K →\to ∼{\sim}1.12M lines of Rust, 89 →\to 126 crates) in one quarter—memories, Guardian, marketplace plugins, code mode, realtime voice; Mistral Vibe grew 77% (35.6K →\to 63K lines); OpenHands re-architected into an SDK while its application repo became an automation control center; Gemini CLI announced its brand pivot and gated its free tier; Aider, the field’s pioneer, settled into community maintenance with 18 commits in the window. Three of the April edition’s observations required substantive revision in place—the coupling dichotomy (Observation 7.1), the size-implies-sandbox correlation (Observation 10.2), and the protocol placement story (Observation 13.3)—each corrected by evidence that did not exist, or that we could not see, ninety days earlier. The methodological lesson generalizes: in this field, inventory claims (tool counts, feature cells, version pins) decay in weeks, while structural claims (loop taxonomy, subsystem anatomy, the absences) have so far proven durable. We have separated the two accordingly throughout this edition.

Observation 12. The coding-agent harness completed its platform turn in the first half of 2026, and every layer of the turn is now visible in source: extension substrates (hooks, skills, plugins) converged across all production systems; capability distribution acquired marketplaces, registries, trust tiers, and agent authors. Vendors shipped importers for each other’s on-disk state and MDM-grade governance layers; the harnesses became importable SDKs while the framework vendors shipped harnesses (the merger of Section 14.2); the agent itself became addressable as a model behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint; and a meta-harness now orchestrates a fleet of eleven vendor harnesses—five of the systems studied here among them—behind one API, re-implementing the expensive parts (sandbox, policy) and arbitraging the proprietary parts (hooks, session stores) of each. The competitive unit of the field is no longer the agent loop; it is the ecosystem surface around it.

15 Discussion

15.1 The Anthropic Effective-Agents Series as Empirical Validation

Between December 2024 and September 2025, Anthropic published four engineering articles offering prescriptive guidance on agent design: Building Effective Agents [16], Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents [19], Writing Effective Tools for AI Agents [18], and the case study How We Built Our Multi-Agent Research System [17]. Across the four pieces, a coherent design philosophy emerges: hand-rolled loops in preference to framework abstractions, a small set of high-signal tools in preference to wrap-everything APIs, just-in-time structural retrieval in preference to pre-indexed RAG, orchestrator-worker patterns in preference to flat monoliths, transparency about agent planning, and explicit context budgeting as an engineering discipline.

Eleven independently developed systems (only one of which, Claude Code, is from Anthropic) line up with these prescriptions:

  • •

    “Don’t use frameworks unless necessary” [16]: 0 of 11 systems use LangChain, LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI, ADK, LlamaIndex, Pydantic AI, Genkit, or Semantic Kernel in the agent runtime (Observation 13.2).

  • •

    “ACI matters as much as HCI” [16] (the concept originates in this article; Aizawa et al. [18] extend it with practical tooling advice) and “few thoughtful tools” [18]: Aider’s 13 polymorphic edit formats, Claude Code’s deferred tool loading, Codex’s custom patch format, Hermes’s nine-strategy edit chain, and OpenCode’s model-conditional tool surfaces are all heavy ACI investments (Observation 8.4).

  • •

    “Just-in-time over RAG” [19]: 0 of 11 systems use vector embeddings over code; all use grep, tree-sitter, glob, and the file system, plus auto-discovered Markdown context files (Observation 13.2).

  • •

    “Orchestrator-workers for parallelizable, context-spanning tasks” [17]: emerges in Claude Code (recursive composition), Codex (thread tree with fan-out), Gemini CLI (registry + session protocol), Mistral Vibe (task tool), OpenHands (parallel delegation), Hermes (orchestrator role + swarm), and OpenCode (concurrent child sessions) (Observation 11.10).

  • •

    “Save plans to external memory before subagent spawn” [17]: Claude Code’s CLAUDE.md, Gemini CLI’s plan files and MEMORY.md project index, Codex’s AGENTS.md hierarchy and its agent-maintained memories root.

  • •

    “Compaction + structured note-taking + sub-agents” for long-horizon tasks [19]: all four provider-native systems—and all three newcomers—implement all three.

  • •

    “Multi-agent systems use ∼\sim15×\times more tokens than chat” [17] (vs. a single chat baseline, not a single-agent pipeline): this is what motivates Claude Code’s prompt-cache-sharing fork mechanism, Hermes’s cache-sharing background forks and summary-only returns, and Gemini CLI’s thought-stripping (extended-thinking text is kept out of persisted history when recording responses, so it never re-enters the cache). Without those optimizations the cost would be prohibitive.

There is one tension in the guidance that we should call out. Hadfield et al. [17] caution that “most coding tasks involve fewer truly parallelizable tasks than research, and LLM agents are not yet great at coordinating and delegating to other agents in real time.” Seven of the eleven systems in this study (eight counting OpenClaw’s protocol-layer variant) nevertheless implement coordinator-worker patterns specifically for coding workflows. On closer inspection the observed patterns are mostly used for breadth-first exploration phases (parallel codebase research) rather than for parallel implementation, which is consistent with Hadfield et al.’s caveat once the unit of analysis shifts from the system as a whole to the individual workflow phase.

15.2 The Minimalism Argument

Mini-SWE-Agent’s competitive self-reported benchmark performance (74%+ on SWE-Bench Verified) with a minimal scaffold and a single bash tool undercuts the assumption that rich tool ecosystems are necessary. The finding echoes the CodeAct [3] argument that executable code subsumes discrete tool actions. For benchmark evaluation alone, most of the scaffolding in the production systems turns out to be overhead.

The counter-argument is that benchmarks measure only a narrow slice of the value proposition. Production systems (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Mistral Vibe, OpenHands) invest heavily in things that benchmarks do not reward:

  • •

    Safety: Preventing destructive actions on user codebases.

  • •

    User experience: Streaming responses, rich terminal UIs, progress tracking.

  • •

    Extensibility: Supporting custom tools, MCP servers, plugins.

  • •

    Robustness: Handling edge cases, stuck detection, error recovery.

  • •

    Cost management: Prompt caching, context compaction, model selection.

These concerns are invisible to SWE-Bench but critical for production adoption.

15.3 Safety as Architecture

Safety is the dimension on which the corpus is most spread out. Codex takes a defense-in-depth approach: OS-level sandboxing plus policy-as-code plus approval workflows, with safety treated as a primary engineering concern from the start rather than as a late addition. Gemini CLI sits at a similar but lighter point on the spectrum: a cross-platform sandbox (reusing OS binaries) plus four explicit approval modes (PLAN/DEFAULT/AUTO_EDIT/YOLO) and per-mode TOML policies. Claude Code’s three-layered system (hooks →\to classifier →\to dialog) sits between pure automation and human oversight. Mistral Vibe’s permission-scope hierarchy (command/file/URL patterns plus agent-profile gates) is more granular than Aider’s binary confirmation but has no OS-level enforcement. OpenHands’s pluggable SecurityAnalyzer framework lets rule-based and LLM-based analysis be combined.

The April edition observed that the corpus’s two largest systems (Codex, then at 621 K lines, and Gemini CLI at 568 K) were also its two cross-platform sandboxers, and read the correlation as structural. The expanded corpus falsifies the structural reading while preserving the cost claim: Hermes and OpenCode are comparably large with zero OS-level isolation, spending their safety budgets on content-borne threats and permission granularity respectively (Observation 10.2). What remains true is that a native sandbox, where built, is among the most code-expensive components in a harness—Codex vendors bubblewrap into its tree, and the meta-harness re-pays the entire bill one layer up (Section 14.4). The minimal safety surface in Aider and Mini-SWE-Agent is defensible for their target use case (developer tools with trusted users) but limits their applicability in enterprise or automated deployment contexts.

15.4 The Model–Agent Co-design Thesis

The coupling between agent scaffolds and foundation models runs in both directions.

The model shapes the agent.

Codex’s per-model prompts—now server-delivered catalog data spanning GPT-5.2 through the 5.6 family, with per-model tool modes and multi-agent tool generations—make explicit that scaffold design has to evolve with model capabilities, and that the vendor intends to drive that evolution without client releases. Claude Code’s extended-thinking integration (budget tokens, thinking blocks) exploits Claude-specific reasoning features. Gemini CLI’s ModelRouterService treats model selection itself as a runtime scheduling decision, dispatching each request to the cheapest sufficient Gemini variant—and absorbing a full model-generation shift (2.5 →\to 3.x defaults) within one quarter; the same idea is studied formally as Hybrid LLM [84], RouteLLM [83], and the FrugalGPT cascade [82]. Mistral Vibe’s reasoning_effort mapping and ThinkChunk parsing exploit Mistral’s reasoning enum. Aider’s model-aware edit format selection adapts the editing strategy to each model’s output patterns, and OpenCode re-derives the same idea in its tool registry (GPT-family models get a patch DSL; others get string replacement) and its nine-prompt model-family matrix. OpenHands ships model-specific tool presets (default, gemini, gpt5, planning)—co-design reaching even a multi-provider system’s tool surface.

The agent shapes model usage.

Claude Code’s deferred tool loading reduces prompt tokens, changing the model’s effective context window. Claude Code’s prompt-caching boundary splits the system prompt to maximize cache hits, structuring the prompt around cache economics as much as around logical organization; Gim et al. [81] provide the systems-level grounding for the modular attention-reuse strategy this implicitly assumes. Gemini CLI keeps extended-thinking traces out of persisted history at response-recording time, so they never leak into future cache lookups (and strips thought signatures on auth switch). Mistral Vibe’s middleware pipeline lets per-turn token-budget policies be composed orthogonally to the loop body. OpenHands’s condensers selectively forget events, shaping what the model “remembers.”

Implications.

The four provider-native systems (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Mistral Vibe) can optimize both sides of this coupling at once, evolving prompts, tools, and features in lockstep with model updates—Codex most literally, via its server-delivered model catalog. The April edition inferred that multi-provider systems must therefore design for the lowest common denominator; the expanded corpus shows that inference was too strong. Hermes, Pi, and OpenCode demonstrate that the full provider-native optimization menu is reachable from a multi-provider substrate by paying the per-provider conditional-code cost deliberately and centrally (Observation 7.1)—per-model quirk metadata, provider-profile plugins, transform matrices. What the multi-provider systems cannot replicate is the update loop: only the vendor can re-tune scaffold behavior server-side on model-release day. Mistral Vibe’s provider-first-with-generic-fallback design and the owned-transports position both remain viable middle paths, differing in who carries the maintenance burden.

15.5 The Scaffold–Capability Frontier (a Guiding Intuition)

We close with a guiding intuition rather than a formal hypothesis: across a fixed task distribution and a fixed model, scaffold complexity and observed task success appear to trace a roughly concave curve. A floor below which the agent cannot operate at all (no loop, no tool, no memory, no result), a steep early-gain region where adding a small set of structural elements (a bash tool, a read/write tool, a Markdown context file) raises success rapidly, and a diminishing-returns plateau where further scaffold work pays off in operational concerns (safety, UX, extensibility) rather than in completion rate. We label this picture the scaffold–capability frontier and treat it as a hypothesis to be tested, not as a proven property of the design space.

Two independent results in the literature are consistent with this picture without confirming it. Mini-SWE-Agent’s reported ∼\sim74%+ on SWE-Bench Verified with a deliberately minimal scaffold suggests that, for SWE-Bench-style tasks on a frontier model, the floor is already well below most production scaffolds. Lin et al. [85] report that their Agentic Harness Engineering (AHE) system, starting from a bash-only seed comparable to Mini-SWE-Agent and automatically evolving the harness using observability-driven feedback, reaches 71.9% on SWE-Bench Verified. Their component-level ablation finds that structural harness elements carry the improvement (tools +3.3+3.3 pp, middleware +2.2+2.2 pp, long-term memory +5.6+5.6 pp), while the system prompt alone regresses performance (−2.3-2.3 pp); the evolved harness also transfers across four model families. We read this as suggestive evidence that structural scaffold is more portable than prose-level prompt strategy, consistent with our model–agent co-design discussion at the architectural (rather than weights) level.

What an operational definition would require is at minimum: a fixed task distribution TT, a fixed model MM, a metric for scaffold complexity (LoC, tool count, structural feature count, or some weighted combination), and a target success rate pp. A “minimum viable scaffold for (T,M,p)(T,M,p)” would then be the lower envelope of scaffold-complexity values whose empirical success rate on TT with MM exceeds pp. We do not produce such a measurement here. Doing so would require a controlled cross-system run study that this paper deliberately avoids (see Threats to Validity, Section 15). We flag the scaffold–capability frontier as a question for follow-on empirical work, and note that the relevant minimum almost certainly varies across:

  • •

    Task complexity: Multi-file refactoring may require more sophisticated tool support than single-file bug fixes.

  • •

    Safety requirements: Enterprise deployments demand scaffolding that benchmarks don’t measure.

  • •

    Interaction patterns: Long-running interactive sessions benefit from memory management that short benchmark runs don’t need.

15.6 Threats to Validity

A study of this shape has real limits, and it is worth being explicit about them.

The analysis rests on source-code reading, not runtime measurement. We do not claim to know how fast any of these systems are; we claim to know how they are structured. Where the paper reports benchmark numbers, they come from the systems’ own documentation, and the last decimal place is not the interesting part.

The qualitative scoring underlying the architectural comparisons involves judgment calls. We tried to anchor each score in a specific implementation detail, and we welcome disagreement from anyone who reads the same codebases and scores them differently. We deliberately avoid line-number citations, and we date all code-size figures to the July-2026 pins: every system in the corpus is actively developed, and finer precision would be obsolete by the time the paper is read. All versions are pinned to exact release tags and commits (Table 3), the April-2026 snapshots are retained for the longitudinal comparison of Section 14.5, and—a lesson that quarter taught us directly—we now distinguish inventory claims, which we date, from structural claims, which we expect to endure. Three observations of the April edition were substantively revised in this one on new evidence; the revisions are integrated in place and flagged where they occur.

The Claude Code analysis is the weakest link on reproducibility. It draws on a publicly circulated source snapshot from March 2026 rather than an official release, and the shipping binary has evolved considerably since (we track its changelog-level evolution but do not treat changelog claims as source evidence). The architectural claims should still be testable against the public claude-agent-sdk and the behavior of the shipping binary, but we acknowledge the asymmetry with the other ten systems, whose source trees are trivially re-derivable from public Git history.

The framework-absence finding (Observation 13.2) is strong but structurally conservative. We checked dependency manifests and performed import grep across three languages—twice, three months apart, across twelve trees including the meta-harness; we did not trace internal forks, plugins loaded via dynamic importlib/require, or transpiled distributions. A company could in principle use LangChain inside a production SWE agent through a code path we did not inspect. We would be surprised, but not shocked.

The Anthropic-guidance-to-observation mapping (Observation 13.2) is suggestive but does not by itself establish causation. The right follow-up is interview work with engineers at each vendor; we did not do that.

We also compared each system independently rather than running all eleven on a shared task set. A head-to-head execution study would turn some of the qualitative scoring into measurable quantities. It would also cost an order of magnitude more effort than this paper, and we chose the tractable scope.

16 Design Recommendations: A Practitioner’s Guide

The preceding sections are descriptive, cataloging what the eleven production harnesses actually contain. This section is prescriptive: we distill the observations into actionable recommendations for an engineer designing a new coding agent. Each recommendation cites the observations that support it, names the systems that implement it, and identifies the trade-off that might justify a different choice. Where the corpus agrees with the Anthropic Effective Agents series [16, 19, 18, 17], we flag the agreement as cross-source validation. Where the corpus diverges from or extends the series, we note that too. The recommendations are grouped by subsystem and ordered roughly in the sequence a practitioner would encounter them when bootstrapping an agent.

16.1 Loop Architecture

Recommendation 1. Start with a linear while loop; graduate to a middleware pipeline only when orthogonal turn policies emerge. Evidence: Observation 5 (loop sophistication does not predict benchmark performance); Mini-SWE-Agent’s 50-line linear loop reports 74%+ on SWE-Bench Verified (self-reported; see the footnote to Table 4). Upgrade path: once you need three or more independent turn-level policies (turn limits, cost caps, auto-compaction, context-budget warnings, read-only mode), adopt Mistral Vibe’s middleware pipeline pattern—each policy becomes a composable middleware, not a new branch in the loop body.

16.2 Provider Coupling

Recommendation 2. If you ship a foundation model, couple tightly to your home provider and expose a generic fallback adapter for portability; if you don’t, provider-native optimizations are still on the table—budget for per-model metadata instead. Evidence: Observation 7.1. Mistral Vibe’s “provider-first with generic fallback” remains the vendor pattern. For multi-provider harnesses, Pi’s per-model compat quirk flags, Hermes’s declarative provider profiles, and OpenCode’s transform matrix show that cache breakpoints, thinking tiers, and reasoning effort are reachable from an abstraction—the cost is a maintained per-provider conditioning layer, paid once and centrally.

16.3 Tool Design

Recommendation 3. Begin with just a bash tool. Add more tools only in response to observed failure modes. Evidence: Mini-SWE-Agent’s single-tool design reports 74%+ on SWE-Bench with essentially no tool infrastructure (self-reported); Aizawa et al. [18] caution that “more tools don’t always lead to better outcomes.” A common sequence is: add read_file and write_file when bash output truncation becomes a problem; add grep/glob when bash+find/rg feels awkward; add search_replace when full-file writes waste tokens.

Recommendation 4. When your tool count exceeds ∼\sim15, adopt deferred tool loading. Evidence: Claude Code’s shouldDefer flag + ToolSearchTool reduces the initial prompt by ∼\sim40%; Codex independently converged with defer_loading flags plus a BM25-ranked tool_search; Hermes collapses overflowing MCP catalogs into three BM25-searched bridge tools once schemas would exceed 10% of the context window. Below ∼\sim15 tools the indirection is not worth the added complexity; above it, the prompt bloat becomes prohibitive.

16.4 File Editing

Recommendation 5. Match your edit-tool contract to your model tier: exact unique-substring replacement for frontier models, a fuzzy cascade for open or weaker models—and in either case handle drift at the tool, never by line numbers. Evidence: Observation 8.4. The frontier-model camp has converged on exact contracts (Claude Code; Mistral Vibe deleted its SEARCH/REPLACE tool and converged on exact matching mid-2026; Pi adds only Unicode/whitespace canonicalization with byte-fidelity overlay). The drift-tolerant camp serves broader model ranges (OpenCode’s nine-stage cascade at Levenshtein 0.65, Hermes’s nine-strategy chain, Aider’s RelativeIndenter). Gemini CLI’s LLM edit-fixer subcall is the emerging third option: repair the match with a model instead of a threshold. Avoid line-number-based edits: models drift on line numbers more than on contextual matching.

16.5 Memory and Context

Recommendation 6. Auto-discover hierarchical Markdown context files at project, user, and extension scopes—and read your neighbors’ filenames too. Evidence: all eleven systems that manage repo context converged on the pattern, and the newest ones read multiple conventions (Hermes: own file, then AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules; OpenCode: AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md/CONTEXT.md plus remote URLs; OpenHands ingests three ecosystems’ files as scoped rules). Inject top-level content near the top of the system prompt, surface nested files just-in-time when tools touch their subtree (Mistral Vibe, OpenCode, Hermes, Gemini CLI), and let the model persist durable facts—by direct edits, bounded snapshot files, or a human-reviewed inbox (Observation 9.6).

Recommendation 7. Implement threshold compaction at a fixed buffer below the model’s context window; preserve a verbatim recent tail; merge summaries incrementally rather than re-summarizing; and wire the same routine to fire reactively on overflow. Evidence: Claude Code fires below a 13 K-token buffer and post-restores files; Gemini CLI compacts at 50% preserving the last 30%; Pi and OpenCode pass the previous summary back for merging (anchored/iterative summaries), which preserves early decisions that from-scratch re-summarization loses; Mistral Vibe re-injects prior user messages into the compacted envelope and reuses the routine on mid-turn ContextTooLong errors; OpenHands routes overflow errors into condensation. Aggressive compaction protects against context rot [19]; conservative preservation keeps recent reasoning coherent.

Recommendation 8. Do not build RAG over code. Use ripgrep, glob, tree-sitter symbol extraction, and file-system traversal instead. Evidence: Observation 13.2; 0/11 systems use vector embeddings for code retrieval; Rajasekaran et al. [19] favor JIT retrieval in practice, and all their concrete recommendations point toward deterministic tools. Code has rich deterministic structure (paths, language servers, tree-sitter parses) that semantic similarity cannot replicate, and changes minute-to-minute, making embeddings stale.

16.6 Safety Architecture by Deployment Context

Recommendation 9. For a developer tool (semi-trusted) context: implement a three-mode approval system (PLAN / DEFAULT / YOLO) with permission-scope patterns. Evidence: Gemini CLI’s PLAN/DEFAULT/YOLO modes, Mistral Vibe’s 4-layer permission hierarchy (tool-wide + tool-specific + session rules + interactive callback); matches how a human developer triages risk.

Recommendation 10. For enterprise / shared / automated contexts: implement OS-level sandboxing with policy-as-code and per-agent audit trails. Evidence: Observation 10.2; Codex and Gemini CLI ship native cross-platform sandboxes (Bubblewrap on Linux—vendored in Codex’s case—Seatbelt on macOS, restricted tokens on Windows), and Claude Code wraps Anthropic’s reusable sandbox-runtime as an opt-in. Gemini CLI’s implementation shows the cost is tolerable when you reuse OS binaries (Node child_process or equivalent) rather than writing namespace plumbing from scratch.

Recommendation 11. Regardless of tier, codify safety rules as data or dedicated policy files rather than as imperative code—and if you support a YOLO mode, keep a floor beneath it. Evidence: Codex’s Starlark execpolicy rules with parse-time-validated inline examples, Claude Code’s PreToolUse hooks, Gemini CLI’s per-mode TOML, OpenCode’s last-match-wins rulesets. Hermes adds the floor lesson: its twelve hardline patterns survive --yolo, with the bypass flag frozen at module import so injected content cannot flip it at runtime. Policies-as-code survive refactors and are auditable independently of the loop implementation.

16.7 Multi-Agent Orchestration

Recommendation 12. Stay single-agent until you can point to a concrete breadth-first exploration phase where parallel context isolation clearly beats serial search. Evidence: Hadfield et al. [17] caution that multi-agent systems use ∼\sim15×\times more tokens than a chat baseline and that “most coding tasks involve fewer truly parallelizable tasks than research”; Mistral Vibe’s task tool delegates to sub-agents (its prompt encourages launching several in parallel), which is sufficient for most coding workflows.

Recommendation 13. Ship an ACP server: it is no longer just an editor integration—it makes your harness consumable by hosts and meta-orchestrators. Keep your own sub-agents in-process. Evidence: Observation 13.3. An ACP server now buys three audiences at once: IDEs (Zed, JetBrains), hosting harnesses (OpenHands runs Claude Code/Codex/Gemini CLI as interchangeable ACP backends), and meta-harnesses (Omnigent drives Goose and Qwen over ACP). Six of eleven corpus systems ship it. For agent ↔\leftrightarrow agent mesh topologies, A2A remains Gemini CLI’s bet alone—defensible, unproven. For main-agent ↔\leftrightarrow sub-agent coordination within your own runtime, do not adopt either (see Recommendation 12): in-process primitives are what production systems use, and even the cross-process exceptions (Pi’s JSONL extension, Hermes’s SQLite-blackboard swarm) avoid the standard protocols for that role.

16.8 Extensibility

Recommendation 14. Use Skills for capability templates (workflows, domain knowledge, procedural recipes) and MCP for external integrations (Slack, databases, internal APIs)—in that order of priority. Evidence: Observation 12.5: skills now lead MCP in adoption (9/11 vs. 8/11), discovery is cross-vendor (OpenCode reads ~/.claude/skills), and distribution has registries and provenance. MCP remains the right layer for running external processes; Pi demonstrates the defensible minimal position (skills plus CLI tools with READMEs, no MCP). If you install third-party skills, treat them as packages: trust tiers, scanning, and quarantine (Hermes) are the emerging baseline [89].

16.9 What Not to Build (Anti-Patterns)

Recommendation 15. Do not use LangChain, LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI, LlamaIndex, Pydantic AI, Genkit, Google ADK, or Semantic Kernel for the agent runtime. Evidence: Observation 13.2; 0/11 production harnesses in the corpus use these frameworks—Gemini CLI skips Google’s own. Schluntz & Zhang [16] explicitly warn: “frameworks often create extra layers of abstraction that can obscure the underlying prompts and responses, making them harder to debug.” Use raw SDK calls—or, the 2026 corollary (Section 14.2): if you want a batteries-included starting point, the harness SDKs (Claude Agent SDK, openai-codex, openhands-sdk) are the framework layer now, with the corpus’s patterns built in.

Recommendation 16. Do not build a vector-embedding retrieval layer for code. Evidence: Observation 13.2; 0/11 systems do this. The embeddings that do appear serve conversation memory (OpenClaw’s default hybrid search; Hermes’s opt-in plugins), and Hermes shows lexical SQLite FTS5 sufficing for that role at 642K-line scale. If you believe your domain needs semantic code retrieval, first prove it improves over ripgrep+tree-sitter on a held-out task set before adding the infrastructure.

Recommendation 17. Do not wrap every upstream SaaS API as a 1-to-1 tool. Evidence: Aizawa et al. [18]; “a common error we’ve observed is tools that merely wrap existing software functionality or API endpoints.” Consolidate instead.

Recommendation 18. Do not over-engineer stuck detection—but do ship the cheap caps, which cost a dozen lines. Evidence: Claude Code and Codex still ship no automated stuck detection and deliver production-quality agents. The floor moved, though: even Mini-SWE-Agent now caps consecutive malformed responses and wall-clock time, OpenCode’s doom-loop check is a three-identical-calls counter routed to a permission ask, and Hermes hashes call signatures but ships the hard stop disabled, trusting warnings. OpenHands’s five-scenario StuckDetector and Gemini CLI’s hybrid hash+LLM service remain platform-tier investments.

16.10 A Minimum Viable Harness

As a concrete starting point, Listing 3 sketches a minimum viable harness in ∼\sim90 lines of Python, combining the patterns recommended above: linear loop (Mini-SWE-Agent), middleware-style policies (Mistral Vibe), four-tool surface (bash, read, write, search_replace), hierarchical Markdown context auto-discovery (all four provider-native systems), and threshold compaction (Claude Code/Gemini CLI/Mistral Vibe). It is not a drop-in library; it is a scaffold to be copied and specialized.

The scaffold above deliberately omits features for which our corpus shows divergence: sandbox (Recommendations 9–10 are deployment-specific), multi-agent (Recommendation 12 defers it), MCP/Skills (Recommendation 14 is extensibility, not core). Start here, measure [17], add the minimum that your observed failure modes demand.

Observation 13. The 90-line minimum viable agent in Listing 3 implements 10 of the 18 recommendations directly and is compatible with the remaining eight. It does so with no framework dependencies, no RAG, no vector store, no multi-agent orchestration, and no sandbox, which lines up with the twin absences (Observation 13.2) and the “start simple” principle of [16]. We conjecture, without proof, that this scaffold running on a frontier model would match Mini-SWE-Agent’s SWE-Bench numbers, and that moving beyond those numbers is primarily a model-capability question (Observation 5) rather than a scaffold question.

17 Conclusion and Future Work

This paper has laid out a source-code-level anatomy of eleven LLM-powered coding harnesses—one per major commercial LLM provider (Claude Code/Anthropic, Codex/OpenAI, Gemini CLI/Google, Mistral Vibe/Mistral) plus seven open-source designs—together with a meta-harness contrast point, a longitudinal diff of one quarter’s evolution, and an account of the field’s turn into platforms.

17.1 Key Takeaways

  1. 1.

    Architecture matters, but not in the way the current discourse implies. The sophistication of the agent loop does not predict benchmark performance (Mini-SWE-Agent’s 50-line loop reports results in the frontier range). It does, however, predict production readiness: safety infrastructure, user experience, extensibility—and increasingly clients and transport, where the largest systems now carry most of their mass.

  2. 2.

    The model–agent relationship is co-evolutionary, and coupling is about the update loop, not capability. Provider-native optimizations (cache boundaries, thinking budgets, model-specific prompts, routing) are exercised from both ends of the coupling spectrum: the vendor systems natively, and Hermes, Pi, and OpenCode from multi-provider substrates by paying the per-provider conditioning cost centrally. What only vendors retain is server-side co-evolution—Codex re-tunes prompts, reasoning tiers, and even its multi-agent tooling per model release from a catalog endpoint, no client update required.

  3. 3.

    Safety is architecturally expensive—and a choice, not a consequence of scale. Codex’s cross-platform sandboxing (now with vendored bubblewrap) remains a substantial investment benchmarks never measure, and the meta-harness re-pays the same bill one layer up. But the April size-implies-sandbox correlation broke: Hermes and OpenCode are among the largest systems with zero OS-level isolation, spending instead on content-borne threat defense and syntax-aware permissioning.

  4. 4.

    Multi-agent orchestration converged on hierarchical patterns, and the protocols found a third role. Coordinator-worker shapes now appear in seven systems. ACP serves not only the editor ↔\leftrightarrow agent boundary (six corpus adopters) but a role outside its design brief: harness hosting, with OpenHands running Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini CLI as interchangeable backends. A2A remains Gemini CLI’s cross-vendor mesh bet. Sub-agent coordination stays in-process in eight of the nine multi-agent systems.

  5. 5.

    The extensibility standards resolved: skills lead. Skills (9/11 systems) overtook MCP (8/11) when Pi broke the tie—implementing agentskills.io while rejecting MCP outright. The skills layer acquired registries, trust tiers, provenance verification, cross-vendor discovery (OpenCode reads ~/.claude/skills), and its first agent authors (Hermes’s self-improving loop, Gemini CLI’s extraction inbox).

  6. 6.

    The twin absences are real, re-verified, and now historically explained. Across eleven systems and roughly four million lines, no agent runtime uses a general-purpose agentic framework, and none uses RAG over code—all rely on hand-rolled async loops and deterministic structural retrieval. The absence held through a threefold corpus expansion and a three-month re-audit, corroborating Anthropic’s published guidance [16, 19] and the independent AHE result [85]. Its resolution is the harness–framework merger of Section 14.2.

  7. 7.

    The Anthropic effective-agents series anticipates the architectures we observe. The four engineering articles published between December 2024 and September 2025 map closely onto the patterns documented across eleven independently developed systems. Whether this reflects shared empirical reality, guidance-shaped design, or both is a question worth pursuing on its own.

  8. 8.

    The analysis is directly actionable. Section 16 distills 18 concrete, evidence-anchored design recommendations for practitioners building new harnesses, together with a 90-line minimum-viable-harness scaffold (Listing 3) that implements ten of them directly. Combined with the source-code audit, this is, as far as we know, the first evidence-based how-to for the discipline that is not a single-vendor whitepaper.

  9. 9.

    The platform turn is no longer a hypothesis. What the April edition advanced cautiously as the CLI-as-framework hypothesis, Section 14 now documents as an accomplished turn: the harnesses ship as importable SDKs while the framework vendors ship harnesses (the merger of Section 14.2); capability distribution has marketplaces, registries, trust tiers [89], and agent authors; vendors write importers for each other’s on-disk state and expose MDM-grade (mobile-device-management) governance; the agent itself is addressable as a model behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint; and a meta-harness orchestrates eleven vendor harnesses—five of the systems studied here among them—behind one API (Section 14.4). The surrounding ecosystem data points the same way: MCP’s 8 000+ server ecosystem with app-store curation pathologies [86], skills formalized as composable packages [87] with npm-like package managers [88], 22–29% of GitHub projects bearing agent traces [91], and the “SE 3.0” framing of development as orchestration [92]. The developer no longer programs with the framework but inside it, and the vendor lock-in of Observation 7.1 is becoming the structural lock-in that operating systems and IDEs have always produced [90]—with the meta-layer already arbitraging it. Whether harnesses consolidate into a few dominant platforms, fragment into interoperable runtimes, or commoditize from above is the competitive question of the next year; the architectural preconditions for all three outcomes are in the source code today.

17.2 Future Work

Several directions emerge from our analysis:

  • •

    Unified evaluation frameworks that assess safety, user experience, cost efficiency, and extensibility alongside correctness, addressing the gap between benchmark performance and production readiness.

  • •

    Reference architecture specification that formalizes the patterns we identified (event sourcing, policy-as-code, context forking, deferred tool loading, middleware pipelines, hash-based loop detection, JIT repo context) into a reusable architectural framework.

  • •

    Formal verification of safety policies for policy-as-code systems, establishing guarantees about what agent actions are permitted under given policy configurations.

  • •

    Empirical study of model–agent co-evolution, tracking how agent scaffolds change across model generations and quantifying the performance impact of model-specific optimizations. Lin et al.’s AHE system [85] demonstrates that automatic harness evolution is already feasible; longitudinal studies could now track how automatically evolved scaffolds compare to hand-crafted ones across model generations.

  • •

    Cross-system benchmark suite that runs identical tasks across all eleven systems under controlled conditions, enabling direct comparison of the architectural trade-offs we identified.

  • •

    Inter-agent protocol adoption study, tracking ACP’s three roles (editor integration, harness hosting, and—via A2A—the cross-vendor mesh) and measuring the overhead of hosted-harness topologies such as OpenHands’s ACP backends and Omnigent’s adapter fleet.

  • •

    Longitudinal continuation: the April/July snapshot pair turns this study into a time series; quarterly re-pinning would measure pattern-diffusion half-lives, prompt thinning, and the platformization trajectory quantitatively rather than anecdotally.

  • •

    Meta-harness economics: whether commoditization-from-above (Section 14.4) captures value durably, and whether the conformance-bench approach to harness capabilities becomes a standard interface.

  • •

    Causation analysis of the Anthropic–industry alignment via interviews, design-doc archaeology, and commit-history correlation, distinguishing public-guidance influence from convergent engineering.
